desc:
You start with a binary search tree with distinct values and apply a list of operations in order. Each operation is a pair [type, value]:

  • [1, v]: insert v as a new leaf, found by the usual walk (go left if smaller, right if larger, attach at the first missing child). If v is already in the tree, do nothing.
  • [2, v]: delete v. If v is not in the tree, do nothing.

Deletion rule. To delete a node: if it is a leaf, remove it; if it has exactly one child, replace the node by that child (the child's whole subtree moves up); if it has two children, copy into it the smallest value of its right subtree (its inorder successor) and then delete that smallest node from the right subtree, which by construction has at most one child. If the key is not in the tree nothing changes.

Return the final tree in the level-order encoding. The rules make the shape of the tree unique.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14] is the tree whose root 8 has children 3 and 10; node 3 has children 1 and 6; node 10 has no left child and right child 14.

Example 1

tree = [4,2,7,1,3], ops = [[1,5],[2,2],[2,4],[1,9]]
Output: [5,3,7,1,-1,-1,9]
After inserting 5: 5 is the left child of 7. Deleting 2 (two children) copies its successor 3 up and removes the old 3. Deleting the root 4 copies the smallest value of its right subtree, 5, to the root and removes that leaf. Finally 9 becomes the right child of 7.

Example 2

tree = [], ops = [[1,3],[1,1],[2,3],[2,8]]
Output: [1]
After deleting the root 3 (one child) the node 1 becomes the root; deleting 8 does nothing.

Example 3

tree = [2,1,3], ops = [[1,2],[2,1],[2,3],[2,2]]
Output: []
constraints: 0 ≤ number of nodes in the initial tree ≤ 3,000
0 ≤ node value ≤ 100,000, all values distinct; the tree is a valid BST
0 ≤ ops.length ≤ 3,000; each operation is [1, v] or [2, v] with 0 ≤ v ≤ 100,000
The number of nodes never exceeds 6,000 during the process
hints: Each operation is one of the two classic BST routines. Write them once on a node-link representation instead of on the raw array.

Decode the array into arrays val, left, right (index = position in level order). New nodes are appended, deleted nodes just become unreachable. Keep a variable for the root, because deleting the root can change it.

For delete: find the node and its parent; with at most one child redirect the parent's link; with two children copy the minimum of the right subtree into the node and splice that minimum out. Encode the final tree with a breadth-first walk and trim trailing -1s.
editorial: Keep the tree as three parallel arrays (value, left index, right index) with -1 for 'none' and a separate root variable. Insert walks down and attaches a new index at the first missing child (or becomes the root of an empty tree); a duplicate is detected when the walk meets an equal value. Delete finds the node while tracking the parent link, handles the zero/one-child cases by redirecting that link (or the root), and for two children copies the successor value and splices the successor node out of the right subtree.
Every operation costs O(h). A path-shaped tree gives h up to n, so the worst case is O(n) per operation, which is fine for these limits. The final breadth-first dump is linear in the number of nodes.
